quote.text: Mara was added to the syllabus and even incorporated into pushing hands.

sections.b:
Mara is Shizenryu's own kata — a structured solo routine created by Ian to give disciplined, Japanese-style solo training without the need to learn a long list of kata that often repeat the same movements. It focuses on the essential tools and body movements required for the partner work of Kumite. It is essentially a solo boxing drill that develops:

  • Breath timing
  • Balance
  • Weight shifting
  • Rotational movement
  • Posture and alignment
  • Flow of defence and counter strike
  • Efficiency of movement

It began as a task: one solo karate routine to shape up a club strong in sensitivity but light on structure, drilled every Sunday until it earned its place in the syllabus. It is the first kata a Shizenryu student learns and the last one they stop refining.

Mara is learned in numbered stages that track the belts: Mara 1–4 at 9th Kyu, 1–6 at 8th, 1–8 at 7th, 1–10 at 6th, 1–12 at 5th, and complete from 4th Kyu. From there the kata turns inward: 2nd Kyu asks for mastery over subtle body torsion; Shodan asks for improved movement and transitions. A full run-through takes about one minute.

From the earliest stages, practise pulling back and using mae-geri to change sides. Mara is not only solo work — it feeds directly into partner practice as the Mara reflex flow drill (Hansha Kumite), which must be shown complete from 2nd Kyu. If your Mara is hollow, your contact reflexes will be too.

quote.text: The old masters stated that all Karate begins and ends with Sanchin. It is both basic and advanced.

sections.b: Sanchin is held as the master kata of all the Naha-te systems and, from all that has been studied in Shizenryu, the root of all kata — a lens through which to study every other. Outwardly it appears the simplest of kata: repeated movements, nothing outside the normal range of motion. That appearance is the first lesson.

Sanchin means 'three conflicts'. To the less initiated, simply the battle between mind, body and spirit — but as you peel the onion, more is revealed. The kata carries the sacred geometry of the circle, triangle and square — in the Zen calligraphic image, creation moving from the unity of the circle, through the triangle, to the manifest form of the square. The old kata carry Buddhist numbers the same way: 18, 36, 54, 72, 108 — each reducing to nine.

Opening & closing — Gassho; dantian; as above, so below; split into a duality, return to one (adults, from 9th Kyu). Footwork — three steps forward and back, using the body to open and close the gates: knees, ankles, feet. Section 1 — single-limb coordination, isometric and isotonic. Section 2 — add the pelvic swivel; use the floor to feel flat back and S back. Section 3 — Samsau: coordinate three limbs at the same time with clearly defined movement. Finally, the complete kata with three ratios of breathing, timing matched clearly to the breath. A full run takes about three minutes.

Uechi-ryu and Isshin-ryu perform Sanchin with open hands, Goju-ryu with closed fists, and some Shorin-ryu branches keep an open-hand version. Comparing them — what changes, and what survives every version — is one of the best study exercises an advanced Shizenryu student can do. In pushing hands, the kata comes alive as Sanchin boxing.

quote.text: Six hands — five animals, plus the snake that grips you.

sections.b: Rokushu is the kata of grip releasing. Its name means 'six hands': the five animals, plus the snake that grips you. It is understood as a later development — a play on Sanchin — and is known in Goju-ryu and Uechi-ryu lines as Tensho.

Rokushu enters the adult syllabus at 2nd Kyu, where the complete kata is required, and remains a standing requirement through the Dan grades. A full run takes about two minutes. Its applications live inside the kakie curriculum: crane spreads its wings, crane circles its wings, snake vs tiger, snake vs standing dragon, and at Nidan the contra grips for laying dragon, leopard and crane — Rokushu applications by name.

Treat every movement as a grip being received, neutralised and released. If Sanchin teaches the body its structure, Rokushu teaches the hands their freedom — the two kata are a pair, and the pushing-hands progression runs straight through them: Sanchin boxing, then Rokushu grip releasing.

quote.text: Once in contact, they stay in contact. Very different to the karate being taught around the world.

sections.b: Naifuanchin is the grappling kata. Its name translates as 'internal divided conflict' — the same inner division described in Zen & Karate, written into movement. It holds the same status in the Shorin and Shuri-te systems that Sanchin holds in Naha-te; the presence of both kata across the old lines suggests a single source behind the art.

Naihanchi in Shorin-ryu and Isshin-ryu, part 1 only in Wado-Ryu, and Tekki 1–3 in Shotokan. The best-preserved version studied in Shizenryu was identified with the help of Shoshin Nagamine's The Essence of Okinawan Karate.

Naifuanchin is the summit of the kata curriculum. It first appears at Shodan (Section 1, in the Mon stage-A material) and is a standing kata requirement at Nidan and Sandan, where the NFC grips are studied — sword grip and scabbard grip, single hand. Those same grips are foreshadowed much earlier: Kumite 11 and 12 at 3rd Kyu are built on the crossed-hand sword and scabbard grips with their takedowns. It is also the final stage of the pushing-hands progression: Naifuanchin grappling.
